findings.text: Decoder tail dispatches control operations including conditional jump with return-address save, match-gated failure, completion validation, constructed-type endings with optional repetition and optional action, unconditional and conditional primitive actions, and jump return. Each case either advances program position or transfers control using saved stacks and match flags.

Constructed ending restores saved depth state then branches on definite versus indefinite length. Indefinite form checks input room and requires zero pair terminator, with collection kinds able to resume element iteration. Definite form requires exact consumption, also with collection resume. When action flag is present the registered handler for the ending is invoked over the constructed content slice.
Successful completion requires both the jump stack and the constructed stack to be empty. Any residue is treated as decoding failure.

Many distinct fault classes observed, including input exhaustion, program exhaustion, control stack overflow and underflow, constructed stack overflow and underflow, length mismatch, missing or malformed terminator, oversize length, forbidden primitive indefinite form, tag mismatch, unsupported long tag form, and reserved operation, all converge to a single negative bad-message result with diagnostic logging.
Conditional-fail and set-ending variants require prior match indication. Without it the decoder follows tag-mismatch failure.

Integer encoder accepts only non-negative values and emits tag plus length plus minimal big-endian magnitude, inserting a leading zero when the top bit would otherwise appear set and using a single zero for value zero. It validates output room, propagates error-pointer input, and returns a pointer just past written bytes or an encoded invalid-argument error.
Encoders treat insufficient room, illegal sizes, and invalid arguments as invalid-argument error-pointer results rather than partial writes, and they propagate an incoming error pointer unchanged.

Object identifier sub-identifier encoding uses base 128 big-endian with continuation bit on all but the final byte, trims leading zero groups, handles zero as a single byte with continuation bit set as observed, and fails when no room remains.

Object identifier encoder requires at least two arcs and at most thirty-two, writes tag, combines the leading pair into one byte, encodes the remainder through the digit helper, backfills length, and returns end pointer or error pointer.
First object identifier content byte equals forty times first arc plus second arc.

Length encoder supports short form for small values, one to three byte long forms for larger values, and a single zero byte for negative request indicating indefinite or recode use. It enforces an upper bound and checks available room before each write.
Length boundaries are 0x7f, 0xff, 0xffff and 0xffffff with long-form leaders 0x81, 0x82 and 0x83 indicating one, two or three following length bytes.

Generic tag encoder writes a context constructed tag limited to thirty, encodes length through the shared helper, and either returns after the header for recode mode when payload is absent or validates room and copies payload when present. Recode mode rewinds two bytes and uses dummy room.
Memory copy transfers the given byte count from source to destination in increasing order and returns the original destination.
Octet string encoder writes tag, encodes length through the shared helper, validates remaining room, copies payload, and returns end pointer or error pointer.
Sequence encoder writes constructed tag and length, supports header-only recode when payload is absent by rewinding and using dummy room, otherwise validates room and copies supplied bytes.
Boolean encoder always produces tag plus length plus a single value byte, with length one and value distinguishing true from false, and propagates error-pointer input.
Boolean wire form occupies three bytes with middle length byte equal to one.
Subtree iteration visits every leaf under a given root until the callback reports non-zero or a stop boundary is reached, descending through shortcuts and nodes.

Each node is scanned twice, first invoking the callback for resident leaves then following metadata pointers. Ascent uses back pointers with slot increment and shortcut skipping, which yields progress despite concurrent splits at the cost of possible duplicate visits.
Whole-array iteration starts from the current root, returns zero immediately when empty, otherwise delegates to subtree walk with no stop bound.
Walk outcome distinguishes empty tree, arrival at terminal node, and arrival at divergent shortcut.
Terminal-node result records containing node reference together with numeric level and slot where descent stopped.
Divergent-shortcut result records shortcut reference together with entry level, comparison level, expected segments, and difference mask.
Walk result is a container offering either a terminal-node triple or a divergent-shortcut quintuple.

Walk derives key chunks per level, selects fan-out slot, follows node pointers by advancing level, and validates shortcuts word by word with trimming beyond the skip target. Mismatch yields divergent-shortcut outcome, missing metadata yields terminal-node outcome, absent root yields empty outcome.
Lookup walks to a terminal node then scans all slots for a leaf satisfying caller comparison, returning the first match or null when the walk diverges or no slot matches.

Destruction performs iterative depth-first traversal from the root, freeing leaves through the caller hook when provided then freeing nodes and shortcuts bottom-up, validating parent links and handling empty tree and top-level shortcut cases.
Destruction tolerates an absent operations table by skipping leaf release while still reclaiming nodes and shortcuts.
Lookup and iteration paths perform ordered pointer loads establishing address dependency before dereference. Fragments show no mutual-exclusion acquisition for these read paths.
Release path returns the object to a pool then, when no freeing is already in progress and the deferred pool is non-empty, marks freeing and schedules delayed background work.
Pool occupancy is observed through an ordered read of the counter field.
Return path executes under an interrupt-save guard and chooses per-processor versus boot list based on a cache-enabled static branch.

Per-processor return prepends the object, maintains a batch marker linking toward batch start, increments count, and when capacity is reached transfers one batch first attempting the global pool then the deferred pool while adjusting global usage.
Per-processor return requires interrupts disabled and serializes batch transfer to shared pools with a dedicated spin lock.
